paper_title: SpecMRL: Redesign Matryoshka Representation Learning within Parametric Spectrum

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides a suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with a parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Representation learning has been well-established research topic in the ML community (Chen et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021b) and underpins wide range of downstream applications (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Karpukhin et al., 2020). The growing applications call for more flexible representation schemes that can adapt to varying latency and storage constraints across use cases. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL, Kusupati et al., 2022) was introduced to address this need, offering an approach that can be easily adopted in existing representation learning frameworks. The central idea of MRL is to extend full-dimensional representation learning to set of nested prefixes. In practice, each nested readout is constructed from the leading portion of the full representation. This design enables representations at multiple output dimensions to be learned within single training run. While simple and effective, it does not explicitly ensure that earlier dimensions are better suited for nested readout, motivating more principled design for MRL. For such prefix readout to be effective, the leading dimensions should ideally concentrate the information most useful for compact representations. However, standard MRL provides no explicit constraint for establishing this ordering. Earlier studies (LI et al., 2025; Huy et al., 2026) have sought to improve low-dimensional readouts through cross-dimensional supervision. Yet, these approaches keep the original coordinate system unchanged, which may itself be ill-suited to effective prefix truncation. Figure 1 depicts how more suitable basis can better organize semantic information and improve the quality of low-dimensional representations. This motivates us to rethink how the representation space itself should be organized to better support nested prefix readout in MRL. To this end, we propose SpecMRL, parameter-derived spectral redesign of MRL that organizes the representation space by feature importance. Such an organization better aligns with the prefixbased design of MRL and provides natural foundation for dimension reduction. Starting from These authors contributed equally. Zhongxin Chen was responsible for the design, implementation, optimization, and evaluation of SpecMRL. Songhao Wu proposed the initial idea of SpecMRL and led this project. Corresponding authors. 1Our code is available at https://github.com/CentreChen/spec-mrl. 1 Preprint. Figure 1: Schematic comparison of standard MRL and SpecMRL. Text embeddings are shown as points in the middle, with colors and marker shapes denoting distinct semantic groups. MRL retains coordinate prefixes in the original basis {ei} as compact representations, whereas SpecMRL performs the readout in an ordered spectral basis {ui} derived from the parameter structure of WProj. The 2D views and enlarged neighborhoods of (red star) illustrate how this change better organizes the semantic space and supports more effective low-dimensional representations. backbone representation, SpecMRL differs from standard MRL only in its choice of basis. Figure 1 presents comparative overview of MRL and SpecMRL, highlighting different organizations of representation space for nested readout. Specifically, SpecMRL changes only the representation basis, with standard MRL subsequently applied in the resulting space. Concretely, we introduce matrix WProj and derive from its Gram matrix an ordered spectral basis that serves as the desired coordinate system. Although this is simple in design, direct implementation poses two challenges: (1) the computational overhead of standard eigen solvers and (2) the numerical instability of eigen vector gradients. To address these challenges, we introduce several technical refinements and develop power-iteration-based alternative to approximate the eigen decomposition of the Gram matrix. Our empirical observations further confirm that this design avoids training collapse due to numerical instability while achieving throughput comparable to vanilla MRL. We conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of SpecMRL and provide further insights into its design. Specifically, we evaluate SpecMRL on widely used MTEB datasets (Muennighoff et al., 2022) with backbones from multiple model families. The empirical results show that SpecMRL substantially improves performance at reduced dimensions, outperforming MRL by up to 3.80 points under 16 compression. Beyond these gains, SpecMRL further extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing its full-capacity performance with only half the dimensions. Further validation shows that these gains persist with larger backbones and longer training, confirming the potential of its further scaling. Our analyses also provide initial insights into why SpecMRL is effective. Taken together, these results motivate rethink of the design principles of MRL and we hope it can inspire improvements for future representation learning.

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND: MATRYOSHKA REPRESENTATION LEARNING (MRL)
sections.content: We briefly review how sentence embeddings are obtained and trained with LLMs before the introduction of MRL (Kusupati et al., 2022). Given an input sequence s, the LLM encodes it into contextualized hidden states and aggregates them into dense representation X: = (LLM ([s1, s2, . . . , sn])) . 2 Preprint. Given training batch B, is typically optimized via the following contrastive loss: (X) = 1 (cid:88) log XB exp (cid:0) sim(X, +; )(cid:1) exp (cid:0) sim(X, +; )(cid:1) + (cid:80) XN exp (cid:0) sim(X, ; )(cid:1) , (1) where + and denote the positive and negative samples of X, and controls the temperature of the similarity function sim(, ; ). MRL extends this contrastive learning over set of nested dimensions M, with loss applied at each dimension. Specifically, for any nested dimension M, MRL retains the first entries of as the reduced representation: (m) MRL = X[: , : m], and aggregates the losses across nested dimensions into weighted objective: LMRL = (cid:88) mM wm (cid:16) (m) MRL (cid:17) , (2) (3) where wm denotes the weight assigned to each dimension m. This nested structure motivates the name, Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). Here, the Matryoshka metaphor is motivated by Russian nesting dolls, reflecting the intuition that more informative features should occupy earlier dimensions. Despite this motivation, MRL does not explicitly ensure such an ordering, leaving the distribution of information across dimensions unspecified. Prior work (LI et al., 2025; Yang & Zhao, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025) has also considered this issue, but mainly introduces additional constraints across nested representations instead of directly ordering the feature dimensions. In this paper, we seek to establish refined design principles toward better dimension reduction. Below, we present SpecMRL as refined perspective on how the core motivation behind MRL can be realized.

sections.title: 3.1 SPECMRL: PARAMETRIC SPECTRAL DESIGN FOR IMPROVED MRL
sections.content: In this section, we first present the implementation of SpecMRL and defer its design principles to later sections. By design, MRL relies on heuristic prior that favors earlier dimensions to construct nested representations. SpecMRL breaks this paradigm and recasts MRLs predefined dimension ordering as learnable spectral organization. Specifically, it encodes this latent structure in WProj RDR and recovers an ordered basis from the spectrum of the corresponding Gram matrix: = Eigen(cid:0) WProj (cid:1) , (4) Proj where Eigen() returns the basis , with eigen values ordered as λ1 λ2 λD 0. With this definition, SpecMRL is drop-in modification to MRL, replacing the nested representation (m) with the spectral prefix (m) Spec in each loss term while leaving the rest of the pipeline unchanged. Given the constructed spectrum, the training objective of SpecMRL can be formulated as: LSpec = (cid:88) mM wm (cid:16) (m) Spec (cid:17) . (6) This substitution changes only the construction of nested representations while preserving the vanilla MRL framework, and requires no additional loss terms or modifications to the training pipeline. Conceptually, the learned parameters of WProj can be viewed as an encoding of the embedding-space geometry. From this perspective, SpecMRL may organize feature channels in more principled manner than vanilla MRL, offering one possible explanation for the observed performance gains. sections.title: 3.2 SPECMRL WITH EFFICIENT AND SCALABLE SPECTRAL SOLVER
sections.content: While SpecMRL is simple in design, its naive implementation can involve several subtle technical challenges that are easy to overlook. straightforward approach is to directly decompose the Gram matrix using off-the-shelf numerical tools, such as the built-in eigen solvers in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019), to obtain the spectral basis. However, this is (1) computationally expensive and (2) sensitive to ill-conditioned eigenvalue distribution, making it unsuitable in practice.2 To address these challenges, we approximate the ordered basis in Eq. 4 with streaming poweriteration design. Specifically, we first initialize the basis with the ordered eigen vectors of the initial Gram matrix. Starting from this initialization, each subsequent step updates the previous basis through single matrix multiplication followed by QR orthogonalization (Householder, 1958): (t) = QR (cid:16) (t) ProjW (t) Proj (t1)(cid:17) , (7) where QR returns the orthogonal factor. Gradients propagate through the Gram matrix and QR factorization, while basis (t1) is held fixed. Similar approaches have been explored in optimizer designs to reduce decomposition overhead (Ahn et al., 2025; Vyas et al., 2025). Figure 2 (b) provides PyTorch-style pseudocode for this design. We further validate the convergence of this solver in Appendix by comparing its solved basis against the exact eigen decomposition solution. The benefits of our power iteration design are empirically validated in practice. In particular, our power-iteration design avoids training collapse across all experimental settings with only modest computational overhead. Once training is complete, the spectral basis is fixed and no longer requires recomputation from WProj. As result, SpecMRL incurs only the cost of linear projection at inference time. We provide detailed analysis of both training and inference costs in Section 4.1.3 to further assess the practical efficiency of SpecMRL.

sections.title: 4.1 METHOD ANALYSIS: CLARIFYING DESIGN PRINCIPLES FOR SPECMRL
sections.content: We begin with ablation studies to shed light on the research questions regarding SpecMRL, seeking to validate its effectiveness and provide insights into the design principles behind it.

sections.title: 4.1.3 EFFICIENCY AND NUMERICAL STABILITY
sections.content: The over-parameterized design, together with the complexity of eigen decomposition, naturally raises concerns about SpecMRLs end-to-end efficiency. In practice, power iteration confines most of the additional computation to standard matrix operations supported by modern hardware, keeping the overhead affordable. Moreover, this overhead is inputindependent and remains small relative to the backbone computation. We provide more comprehensive complexity analysis in Appendix E. sections.title: 4.2.1 SPECTRUM CONTRIBUTES BEYOND GRAM-MATRIX OVER-PARAMETERIZATION.
sections.content: Compared with vanilla MRL, SpecMRL introduces learnable factor WProj RDR and derives its ordered spectral basis from the corresponding Gram matrix. To examine whether the improvement can be explained merely by this additional parameterization, we construct an ablated variant that retains the same learnable factor but removes spectral decomposition. For nested dimension m, let Wm = WProj[: m, :]. This variant retains the original coordinate prefixes (m) and evaluates similarity after the implicit lifting (m)Wm. Equivalently, its similarity is induced by the Gram matrix Gm = WmW . We therefore refer to this variant as MRL w. Gram. The full formulation and details are provided in Appendix A.3. As shown in Table 5, the Gram-based variant provides only limited improvements over vanilla MRL In contrast, SpecMRL consistently performs and degrades rapidly under stronger compression. better at reduced dimensions. These results show that introducing the same learnable factor through Gram-based similarity does not reproduce the gains of SpecMRL, supporting the proposed spectral readout over this alternative. Extra comparison with learnable linear is provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4.2.2 EIGEN DECOMPOSITION PROVIDES MORE THAN LEARNABLE ORTHOGONALITY
sections.content: Eigen decomposition organizes the learned structure into an ordered set of orthogonal directions. This suggests two possible sources of improvement: learning favorable orthogonal basis and imposing spectral ordering. To disentangle their effects, we construct an ablated variant that retains only learnable orthogonality. This allows us to assess whether the learned spectral ordering benefits MRLs nested readouts. Specifically, we replace the orthogonal basis in Eq. 4 as: UOrth = QR(cid:0) WProj Proj (cid:1) , (11) where QR is applied to the Gram matrix alone to retain orthogonality. Table 5 (b) reports its results. Compared with vanilla MRL, learned orthogonality provides clear advantage, but remains inferior to the full SpecMRL design. This further highlights the value of ordering feature directions by learned importance, which is naturally compatible with MRLs nested readout design.

Beyond these gains, SpecMRL provides additional advantage in practice, since it only changes the prefix-readout basis. As consequence, this makes SpecMRL compatible extension to MRL, requiring no extra hyperparameter tuning while remaining robust across diverse tasks. Further details for baselines implementation and additional evaluation results are provided in Appendix A.2 for clarity.

sections.title: 4.5 ROBUSTNESS TO MRL CONFIGURATIONS
sections.content: We further evaluate SpecMRL under different MRL settings to assess whether its advantages are robust across configurations. Specifically, we conduct two experiments on Qwen3-0.6B: (1) setting all nested loss weights to 1, and (2) adopting sparse supervision by dropping the last two dimensions (128 and 64) from the nested training set. All other training settings are kept unchanged. Table 9 compares MRL and SpecMRL under different configurations. Across these configurations, SpecMRL consistently preserves the low-dimensional advantage observed in the main experiments, indicating robustness to MRL training settings. Notably, under sparse supervision, SpecMRL achieves larger gains over MRL at the two prefixes without dedicated loss terms, including 7.29point improvement at 64 dimensions. This suggests that SpecMRL depends less on direct supervision at individual prefixes to preserve low-dimensional information, enabling effective readout under sparser nested supervision and demonstrating robustness to the choice of training dimensions. 4.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Modern applications use models to encode data into embeddings for wide range of downstream tasks. Despite continued improvements in quality, the storage and computational costs of fixed, high-dimensional embeddings remain practical bottleneck. MRL (Kusupati et al., 2022) addresses this limitation through joint supervision of nested prefixes, enabling flexible output dimensions. While MRL is simple, several methods seek further improvements by introducing auxiliary objectives. ESE (LI et al., 2025) introduces learn-to-compress (L2C) objective that supervises truncated prefixes with PCA-based compression targets. Similarly, MIPIC (Huy et al., 2026) aligns tokenlevel relations across dimensions through self-distilled intra-relational alignment (SIA), matching token-importance distributions with KL divergence and inter-token geometry with centered kernel alignment. Both methods derive alignment targets from full-dimensional embeddings to supervise low-dimensional prefixes, while also incorporating intermediate-layer supervision to improve embeddings at shallower depths. In contrast to alignment-based supervision, MIC (Hong et al., 2026) introduces geometric regularization to reduce redundancy between prefix and residual dimensions. MRL has also been extended to frozen models by adding lightweight trainable layers, supporting effective prefix truncation at multiple dimensions without backbone update. Following this idea, Matryoshka-Adaptor (Yoon et al., 2024) learns nested embeddings through lightweight adapters, while SMEC (Zhang et al., 2025) further improves this adaptation process through sequential training and adaptive dimension selection. More recently, AdaWidth (Yang & Zhao, 2026) learns an orthogonal rotation of frozen embeddings, providing learnable orthogonal basis without explicit spectral ordering. This design is conceptually closely related to the learnable-basis ablation considered in our analysis, which underperforms the proposed spectral basis. 10 Preprint.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present SpecMRL, parametric-spectral redesign of MRL that addresses the limitations of fixed basis-prefix readout. By exploiting the ordered orthogonal structure of the learned spectrum, SpecMRL reorganizes representations into form naturally suited to nested truncation. Across diverse experimental settings, SpecMRL consistently outperforms MRL at reduced dimensions with negligible overhead, while further extending the performance frontier. These findings highlight the readout space as an important learning target in nested representation. We hope this perspective motivates further exploration of information organization and inspires more principled MRL designs.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 GENERAL SETUP Training Setup. We conduct the main experiments reported in Table 1 using backbones from widely used model families, including Qwen3-0.6B-Base (Team, 2025), Qwen2-0.5B (Yang et al., 2024), and Llama-3.2-1B (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We further include Qwen3-4B-Base in the scaling experiments to evaluate performance at larger model scale. Unless otherwise specified, we instantiate as mean pooling to derive the embeddings. For MRL training setup, we follow the setup of Hu et al. (2025) and summarize the configuration for each backbone in Table 13, where mi denotes the i-th nested dimension and wi denotes its corresponding loss weight. For brevity, τ denotes the compression ratio rounded to the nearest power of two throughout the tables. We provide further details on our training setup. For data preparation, we use the publicly available KaLM-embedding-finetuning-data dataset3 (Hu et al., 2025). By default, we train on randomly sampled subset of 1,152,000 examples, approximately 1/5 of the full dataset, to keep the experimental cost manageable. Specifically, each training example consists of one query, one positive example, and seven hard negatives. We also use in-batch negatives across GPUs. For the long-run experiments in Section 4.3, we use the full dataset to evaluate performance under extended training. Regarding the training hyperparameters, the per-device batch size is set to 96 queries, resulting in global batch size of 384 across four GPUs. We adopt GradCache (Gao et al., 2021a) to reduce memory usage. The maximum sequence length is set to 512 tokens for both queries and passages. We use the AdamW optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2017; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with learning rate of 104, warmup ratio of 0.1 followed by linear decay, and weight decay of 0.01. For contrastive learning, the temperature is set to 0.01 across all experimental settings. We initialize the entries of WProj from (0, 0.022) and obtain the initial spectral basis via the eigenvectors of its Gram matrix. More implementation details and reproducibility information are provided in our codebase. Evaluation. We conduct experiments on the widely used English MTEB benchmark (Muennighoff et al., 2022), which comprises 56 datasets spanning seven task categories: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS.), Classification (Class.), Clustering (Cluster.), Pair Classification (PairClass.), Reranking (Rerank.), Retrieval (Retr.), and Summarization (Sum.). For experiments presented in Figures 3 and 4, we report the average score over 15-dataset evaluation subset detailed in Table 14. For sentence encoding, both MRL and SpecMRL follow KaLMs task-specific inference instructions (Hu et al., 2025). For SpecMRL, we perform one orthogonal iteration in FP32 using the final parameter Gram matrix, starting from the spectral basis saved in the checkpoint. The resulting basis remains fixed throughout evaluation. For Qwen2-0.5B, we use the same nested dimensions for training and evaluation, following KaLM (Hu et al., 2025). We use unnormalized embeddings for classification and apply L2 normalization at each target dimension for all other tasks. A.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION OF ESE AND MIPIC
sections.content: To focus on dimensional compression and facilitate controlled comparison with MRL and SpecMRL, we adapt ESE and MIPIC to use only the final-layer representations of Qwen3-0.6B. Method-specific hyperparameters are selected following the original papers (LI et al., 2025; Huy et al., 2026). The implementations of all baselines are also available in our code repository. Detailed evaluation results for all compared methods are presented in Table 18. ESE (L2C). We retain the learn-to-compress objective and apply it to the final-layer sentence embeddings, omitting intermediate-layer supervision. Contrastive losses are applied to the full 1024dimensional representation and its 128-dimensional prefix. The latter additionally receives alignment supervision from the compression targets. Representations at other dimensions are obtained by prefix truncation at evaluation time, without additional training losses at those dimensions. MIPIC (SIA). We combine the MRL objective with SIA applied to final-layer token representations. The nested dimensions and MRL loss weights follow Table 13. Using mean-pooled sentence 3huggingface.co/datasets/KaLM-Embedding/KaLM-embedding-finetuning-data 15 Preprint. embeddings as anchors, SIA aligns token-importance distributions across dimensions through KL divergence. Linear CKA further aligns the relational structures of full-dimensional and truncated representations on token subsets selected by full-dimensional importance scores. sections.title: C PARAMETER SPACE REFLECTS EMBEDDING GEOMETRY
sections.content: From parametric perspective, each column of WProj can be interpreted as an embedding-space vector, making the weight matrix structurally analogous to cached collection of embeddings. We contend that WProj encodes high-level semantic information, such that their collective organization in parameter space reflects the geometry of the learned embedding space during training. We present our empirical observations to substantiate this structural correspondence. Specifically, we randomly sample = 106 sentences from the training set and encode them separately using MRL and SpecMRL to obtain calibration embeddings ˆEcal RN D. Using these embeddings as reference, we extract their principal directions ˆE and compare the resulting leading k-dimensional subspace with the corresponding readout subspace using principal-angle overlap: Sk = (cid:13) (cid:104)(cid:0)U ˆE (cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:1) 1 (cid:105) U:,1:k :,1:k (cid:13) 2 (cid:13) (cid:13) (cid:13) , (13) where denotes the readout basis of the model. As shown in Table 12, both the overlap scores of MRL and SpecMRL exceed the random baseline, suggesting that the MRL objective encourages alignment between readout subspaces and embedding geometry. Viewed as collection of embedding vectors, the parameter matrix can be interpreted as learned proxy for the full population of sentence embeddings, fitting their geometry during training. sections.title: SpecMRL
sections.content: For SpecMRL, the readout basis used is obtained by power iteration, following the procedure described in Appendix A. We further verify this approximation against the ordered eigenbasis computed directly from the same Gram matrix. At the final checkpoint, their subspace overlap exceeds 99.9% for all evaluated k, indicating that the two bases span nearly identical leading subspaces.

sections.title: D ENERGY CONCENTRATION IN THE TAILING SPECTRAL SUBSPACE
sections.content: We conduct further analyses to investigate why dropping the final spectral bands can improve SpecMRLs downstream performance. Motivated by the analysis in (Wu et al., 2026), we examine the behavior of SpecMRL-derived representations when projected onto different spectral bands. Specifically, we first partition the spectrum into 20 consecutive bands ordered by eigenvalue. We then sample = 106 passages from the MS MARCO corpus (Nguyen et al., 2016) to obtain the calibration embeddings. Let zij = X[i] denote the projection of X[i] onto the j-th spectral direction. (14) Figure 5 shows that the final band accounts for large fraction of energy (21.72%), despite spanning only 5% of the spectral directions. Ideally, the energy should decay smoothly across the ordered spectral bands, with the first band accounting for the largest share, consistent with its intended role in capturing the most informative semantic directions in MRL. The decay pattern reflects the decreasing semantic importance of later spectral bands, while the smoothness helps maintain isotropy by avoiding concentration in small subset of directions. In turn, the disproportionate concentration in the final band indicates increased anisotropy, suggesting departure from the expected geometry. Similar observations have also been reported by Wu et al. (2026). Although the cause of this phenomenon remains unclear, we hope this analysis provides an initial explanation for the observed improvement and motivates further investigation. sections.content: This section provides supplementary analysis of SpecMRLs computational overhead relative to MRL. The additional computations consist of Gram matrix construction and orthogonal basis update, followed by projecting batch of Bproj embeddings of dimension D. As shown in Fig. 2, the orthogonal basis update involves only one matrix multiplication and one QR factorization (Householder, 1958). Counting multiply-add as two FLOPs, the matrix multiplication requires 2D3 3 D3 FLOPs in total: 4 FLOPs, while QR factorization costs 8 3 D3 3 D3 for factorization and another 4 17 Preprint. for explicitly forming the full orthogonal matrix.
